zachow--handel-lessons.title: Zachow joins counterpoint to foreign repertory

works.from: Zachow’s teaching in Halle
works.to: Handel’s childhood training

zachow--handel-lessons.claim: Handel studied with the Halle organist Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow before his later Hamburg apprenticeship. Zachow’s teaching combined counterpoint and figured bass with exposure to Italian and French instrumental music, an unusually concrete basis for Handel’s later command of several national styles.

works.to: Bach’s visit of 1705–06

buxtehude--bach-lubeck.claim: Bach obtained leave from his Arnstadt post in 1705 to visit Lübeck and hear Buxtehude, but remained away into 1706. The subsequent consistory examination records Bach’s explanation that he had travelled to learn things connected with his art: the encounter is supported by an employment dispute, not merely an influence legend.

The opening Adagio states the familiar D-minor melody before the changing tempi and figuration; the source is a shared tradition, not a tune invented by Corelli.

works.from: Hortus musicus, Sonata No. 1
works.to: Sonata in A minor, BWV 965 (c. 1705)

reincken--bach-bwv965.claim: Bach’s A-minor keyboard Sonata BWV 965 adapts Reincken’s first sonata from Hortus musicus, originally ensemble music. The keyboard version retains a succession of introductory, fugal and dance movements: the transmission is an identifiable arrangement, not simply membership of the North German organ school.

works.from: Handel’s keyboard playing in Italy
works.to: Scarlatti’s reported encounter with Handel

handel--scarlatti-roman-contest.claim: The familiar account places Handel and Scarlatti in a keyboard contest at Cardinal Ottoboni’s in Rome, with Handel preferred on the organ. The story belongs to the retrospective anecdotal tradition surrounding their Italian encounters; it is evidence of how their reputations were narrated, not proof that a particular Scarlatti sonata borrows from Handel.

works.from: Premier livre d’orgue (1699; reissued 1711)
works.to: Bach’s copy of Grigny’s organ collection

grigny--bach-livre-orgue.claim: Bach’s autograph copy of Grigny’s Premier livre d’orgue survives in Frankfurt as Mus Hs 1538. In the same manuscript he copied Dieupart’s harpsichord suites and d’Anglebert’s ornament table: French repertory and instructions for playing its ornaments travelled together into his working library.

The two manuals let him distinguish tutti and solo material; added ornaments, middle-voice detail and fuller chords adapt the same concerto architecture to the organ.

frescobaldi--bach-fiori.title: Frescobaldi’s organ Masses reach Bach’s desk

works.from: Fiori musicali (1635)
works.to: Bach’s study copy of Fiori musicali

frescobaldi--bach-fiori.claim: A manuscript of Frescobaldi’s Fiori musicali bore Bach’s name and the date 1714; the volume was subsequently lost during the Second World War. The collection’s chant-based Kyrie versets, canzonas and ricercars gave him access to a specific Italian model of liturgical organ counterpoint, without requiring an invented chain of personal lessons from Frescobaldi to Bach.
frescobaldi--bach-fiori.note: Older accounts call this Bach’s complete autograph copy. The 2026 source cautions that it may instead have been a scribal copy signed and dated by him; ‘copied’ here denotes manuscript transmission, not certainty about the copyist’s hand.

marcello--bach-bwv974.title: An oboe concerto becomes keyboard ornament study

works.from: Oboe Concerto in D minor, S D935
works.to: Keyboard Concerto in D minor, BWV 974 (c. 1713–14)

marcello--bach-bwv974.claim: The source of Bach’s BWV 974 is the D-minor oboe concerto by Alessandro Marcello, not his brother Benedetto. Bach recast the oboe-and-strings texture for one keyboard, preserving its Italian identity while elaborating the ornamented solo line.
marcello--bach-bwv974.note: The transcription is dated approximately 1713–14; the route by which the manuscript reached Weimar is uncertain.

corelli--couperin-parnasse.title: Corelli climbs Couperin’s Parnassus

works.from: Corelli’s instrumental music
works.to: Le Parnasse, ou L’Apothéose de Corelli (1724)

corelli--couperin-parnasse.claim: Couperin’s 1724 trio sonata gives Corelli a programme in seven named movements: he petitions the Muses, drinks at Hippocrene, sleeps, and is placed beside Apollo. The tribute is explicit in the work’s title and movement headings, rather than a resemblance retrospectively assigned by listeners.

couperin--bach-bergeries.title: Couperin enters the Bach family notebook

works.from: Les Bergeries, Second livre, Sixième ordre (1717)
works.to: Anna Magdalena Bach’s 1725 notebook, No. 6, BWV Anh. 183

couperin--bach-bergeries.claim: The rondeau in B♭ major entered as No. 6 in the 1725 Anna Magdalena notebook is Couperin’s Les Bergeries, published in 1717. Its presence documents French harpsichord music in the Bach household, but does not make the piece Bach’s composition or establish him as this entry’s copyist.
couperin--bach-bergeries.note: The year names the notebook; not every entry was necessarily written in 1725. ‘Copied’ describes household transmission, not an authenticated Johann Sebastian autograph.

lully--couperin-apotheose.title: Lully and Corelli reconcile on Parnassus

works.from: Lully’s French instrumental style
works.to: L’Apothéose de Lully (1725)

lully--couperin-apotheose.claim: In Couperin’s 1725 instrumental homage, Apollo persuades Lully and Corelli to unite French and Italian tastes. Two successive headings specify Lully playing the subject with Corelli accompanying, then Corelli playing while Lully accompanies: stylistic reconciliation becomes an audible exchange of roles.

palestrina--fux-aloysius.title: Palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper

works.from: Palestrina’s reputation as a contrapuntal model
works.to: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725)

palestrina--fux-aloysius.claim: Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum presents counterpoint through a dialogue between Aloysius, representing Palestrina, and Josephus, representing Fux. The imagined lesson became a route from the older contrapuntal ideal into the studies of Haydn and Beethoven; it is not a historical claim that Fux met Palestrina.

luther--bach-ein-feste-burg.title: Luther’s hymn becomes a contrapuntal fortress

works.from: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott
works.to: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, BWV 80, Leipzig versions

luther--bach-ein-feste-burg.claim: Bach expanded an earlier Weimar cantata into a Leipzig Reformation cantata using Luther’s Ein feste Burg. In the opening movement the chorale appears in long notes in the instrumental parts while the chorus works around it in imitation; the hymn supplies a structural layer, not just a closing quotation.
luther--bach-ein-feste-burg.note: The Leipzig work developed in stages; 1730 is an approximate timeline anchor, not a fixed premiere date. Wilhelm Friedemann Bach’s later trumpet additions are not treated as his father’s original scoring.

vivaldi--bach-bwv1065.title: Four violins become four harpsichords

works.from: Concerto in B minor, Op. 3 No. 10, RV 580
works.to: Concerto for four harpsichords in A minor, BWV 1065 (c. 1730)

vivaldi--bach-bwv1065.claim: Bach converted Vivaldi’s B-minor concerto for four violins into an A-minor concerto for four harpsichords and strings. Each violin line becomes a two-handed keyboard part; the broken-chord slow movement remains especially close to Vivaldi’s original, despite the changed instrumental sound.
vivaldi--bach-bwv1065.note: Around 1730 is an estimate. The often-imagined performance by Bach and three of his children is not established and is not asserted here.

bach--cpe-bach-only-teacher.title: Emanuel identifies his only music teacher

works.from: Johann Sebastian Bach’s household teaching
works.to: C. P. E. Bach’s training in keyboard and composition

bach--cpe-bach-only-teacher.claim: In the autobiography prepared for Burney and published in 1773, Emanuel Bach identifies his father as his only teacher of composition and keyboard playing. The same document lists his first published keyboard minuet in 1731; the teaching link rests on the pupil’s own testimony, not merely their surname.
bach--cpe-bach-only-teacher.note: 1731 anchors the end of the early-training period to Emanuel’s first listed publication, not the beginning or end of all lessons.

dryden--handel-alexanders-feast.title: Dryden’s musical feast reaches Covent Garden

works.from: Alexander’s Feast, or the Power of Musick
works.to: Alexander’s Feast, HWV 75 (1736)

dryden--handel-alexanders-feast.claim: The Covent Garden advertisement for 19 February 1736 announces a new ode written by the late Dryden and set by Handel. A letter of 24 January already describes Handel playing almost the entire new work to Shaftesbury, who singled out the chorus beginning ‘Happy, happy’: contemporary witnesses identify both the literary source and the composition in preparation.

milton--handel-lallegro.title: Milton’s opposed poems alternate inside Handel’s ode

works.from: L’Allegro and Il Penseroso
works.to: L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato (1740)

milton--handel-lallegro.claim: Charles Jennens selected and interleaved passages from Milton’s companion poems for Handel’s L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato, first performed in London on 27 February 1740. The third part, Il Moderato, is Jennens’s addition, not a third Milton poem: literary adaptation is built into the musical alternation of temperaments.

works.from: Voltaire, La Princesse de Navarre
works.to: La Princesse de Navarre, RCT 44 (1745)

voltaire--rameau-navarre.claim: Rameau supplied the music for Voltaire’s La Princesse de Navarre in 1745. The comédie-ballet has an overture and three acts; its literary author is the same Voltaire better known for philosophical prose, not an anonymous court librettist.

works.to: Tilge, Höchster, meine Sünden, BWV 1083 (1740s)

pergolesi--bach-psalm51.claim: Bach adapted Pergolesi’s Stabat mater to a German paraphrase of Psalm 51 in Tilge, Höchster, meine Sünden, BWV 1083. The music crosses both language and liturgical context: a Latin Marian text gives way to a German penitential psalm.

works.from: Plainchant intonation, Credo in unum Deum
works.to: Mass in B minor, BWV 232, opening Credo

gregorian-chant--bach-credo.claim: Bach based the opening of the B-minor Mass’s Credo on an older chant intonation for the words Credo in unum Deum. He gives the borrowed head-motif measured rhythm and sets it over a walking continuo bass, joining an archaic vocal subject to an active instrumental foundation.

works.from: C. P. E. Bach’s keyboard sonatas

cpe-bach--haydn-sonatas.claim: Haydn recalled playing Emanuel Bach’s sonatas repeatedly during his early years of independent study. The testimony names actual keyboard works as models; it does not say that Haydn was Emanuel’s personal pupil or identify one particular sonata as the source of a later Haydn theme.

works.from: Gradus ad Parnassum (1725)
works.to: Haydn’s self-directed counterpoint exercises

fux--haydn-gradus.claim: Griesinger’s account, reproduced by Nohl, describes Haydn solving Fux’s counterpoint problems, putting them aside, then returning to check them. The method was repeated written work rather than a single encounter with a famous treatise, and Haydn retained a worn copy.

works.from: Spanish plucked-string and dance gestures
works.to: Keyboard Sonata in A minor, K. 175

spanish-guitar-dance--scarlatti-k175.claim: Giulio d’Amore’s Santa Cecilia programme note hears Andalusian guitar attack and dance energy in the dense, dissonant chords of Scarlatti’s K. 175. works.from: Porpora’s vocal and compositional teaching in Vienna
works.to: Haydn’s lessons in the early 1750s

porpora--haydn-lessons.claim: In Vienna, Haydn accompanied pupils in Porpora’s singing lessons and received instruction in return. Porpora’s teaching connected composition with singing and Italian declamation, a practical complement to Haydn’s independent keyboard and counterpoint studies.

works.to: Keyboard Concerto in D major, K. 40, finale (July 1767)

works.from: Keyboard Sonatas Op. 5 Nos. 2–4
works.to: Three keyboard concertos, K. 107 (after 1770)

jc-bach--mozart-k107.claim: Mozart’s three concertos K. 107 transform Johann Christian Bach’s Op. 5 Nos. 2, 3 and 4 into works for keyboard with strings. The surviving manuscript contains work by both Wolfgang and Leopold, so these arrangements document a practical family workshop in concerto writing as well as Wolfgang’s admiration for the London Bach.

van-swieten--mozart-fugue-sessions.title: Sunday sessions bring Bach and Handel home

works.from: Van Swieten’s Bach and Handel repertory
works.to: Mozart’s Prelude and Fugue in C, K. 394 (1782)

van-swieten--mozart-fugue-sessions.claim: In his letter to Nannerl of 20 April 1782, Mozart explains that van Swieten lent him Bach and Handel works after he had played them at the baron’s Sunday gatherings. Constanze’s enthusiasm for fugues then helped prompt the Prelude and Fugue K. 394: the letter supplies a named intermediary and a particular compositional result.

works.to: Beethoven’s keyboard studies in Bonn

bach--beethoven-wtc.claim: Neefe’s communication to Cramer’s Magazin der Musik, dated 2 March 1783, identifies Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier as central to the young Beethoven’s keyboard repertory and says Neefe supplied it. handel--mozart-messias.title: Mozart recolours Messiah for Viennese winds

works.from: Messiah, HWV 56 (1741)

In 1816 Zelter had written to Goethe that her father’s eldest daughter “could give you something of Sebastian Bach”. polish-folk-music--chopin-szafarnia-1825.title: Chopin hears village musicians at Szafarnia, 1825

works.to: Chopin’s mazurkas, from Op. 6 and Op. 7 (composed 1830–31, published 1832)

polish-folk-music--chopin-szafarnia-1825.claim: Chopin spent the summers of 1824 and 1825 at Szafarnia, the Dziewanowski estate, where he met authentic folk music at first hand: he wrote down songs he heard, joined in rural amusements, and in a letter home of 26 August 1825 describes accompanying a fiddler on a one-stringed cello. His first published mazurkas, Op. 6 and Op. 7, date from 1830–31 and appeared in 1832. In 1852 Liszt wrote that Chopin’s mazurkas grew directly out of Polish national music, and later writers read “national” as “folk”; recent scholarship holds instead that the likelier source is the national music Chopin heard in the towns.
polish-folk-music--chopin-szafarnia-1825.note: The Szafarnia summers are documented in Chopin’s own letters. Whether the mazurkas rest directly on village folk music, as Liszt’s 1852 book was read to say, or on the urban national music of Warsaw, is debated; the evidence does not settle which tunes, if any, he took from what he heard in 1824–25.

He calls the evening, in the Mémoires (chapter 18), the “greatest drama” of his life and says Shakespeare, arriving unawares, struck him like a thunderbolt. He married Smithson in 1833, and the plays stayed with him: Roméo et Juliette (1839) and Béatrice et Bénédict (1862, after Much Ado About Nothing) are the largest results.

beethoven-symphonies--berlioz-conservato.claim: The Société des concerts du Conservatoire, directed by François Habeneck, gave its first concert on 9 March 1828, and from then on Paris heard Beethoven’s symphonies played regularly. In his Mémoires (chapter 20) Berlioz says the shock was almost equal to Shakespeare’s: Beethoven opened a new world in music as the poet had opened one in poetry. From 1828 he also studied and copied Beethoven’s scores in the Conservatoire library. Two years later Habeneck conducted the premiere of the Symphonie fantastique in the same hall.

works.to: Mendelssohn’s revival, Berlin Sing-Akademie, 11 March 1829

bach-st-matthew--mendelssohn-berlin-1829.claim: Mendelssohn’s grandmother Bella Salomon had given him a copy of the St Matthew Passion score in the mid-1820s, and his teacher Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Sing-Akademie, held a store of Bach scores but would not perform the work in public. On 11 March 1829, aged twenty, Mendelssohn conducted the Passion at the Sing-Akademie in Berlin, the first performance outside Leipzig. He cut about a third of the arias and half the choruses but few chorales, and the revival is usually counted as the start of the Bach revival.

works.to: Huit scènes de Faust (1828–29); La damnation de Faust (1846)

goethe-faust--berlioz-eight-scenes.claim: Berlioz first read Goethe’s Faust in Gérard de Nerval’s prose translation and says in the Mémoires (chapter 26) that he could not put it down, reading it at table, in the theatre and in the street. He set the translation’s verse fragments as Huit scènes de Faust, had them engraved at his own expense in 1829, then collected and destroyed the copies; the “Concert des Sylphes” was sung at his Conservatoire concert of 1 November 1829. Twenty years later he reworked those ideas into La damnation de Faust, first given at the Opéra-Comique on 6 December 1846.

works.to: Schumann, Papillons, Op. 2 (1829–31)

jean-paul-flegeljahre--schumann-papillon.claim: In April 1832 Schumann explained to the editor Ludwig Rellstab how his Papillons arose: he asked him to recall the last scene of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre, the masked ball, the dancing, the exchange of masks, the confessions and the brother’s departure. He said he kept turning to the last page, “almost unconsciously” found himself at the piano, and one piece after another came into being. In November 1829 he had written to Friedrich Wieck that Schubert was “my only Schubert” just as Jean Paul was “my only Jean Paul”.

On 2 May he wrote to Pierre Wolff that he was practising exercises “four or five hours” a day and studying a long shelf of authors and composers at once. The first result was the Grande fantaisie de bravoure sur La Clochette (1832); the six Paganini études were published in 1838 and revised in 1851, with five of them based on Paganini’s Caprices.

Robert Schumann revised the orchestration of its first movement in 1834; she later undid his changes, orchestrated it herself, and finished the three-movement concerto on 1 September 1835, twelve days before her sixteenth birthday. beethoven-ferne-geliebte--schumann-fanta.claim: Schumann began the Fantasie in 1836 as Ruines, a piece written in his distress at being parted from Clara Wieck. He expanded it into a work to raise money for the Beethoven monument in Bonn, offering 100 presentation copies to the publisher Kistner. The last bars of the first movement quote the phrase “Nimm sie hin denn, diese Lieder” (“Accept, then, these songs”) from Beethoven’s song cycle, a quotation Schumann did not acknowledge and which apparently went unnoticed until 1910. He dedicated the published score, of 1839, to Liszt.

works.to: Schumann, Davidsbündlertänze, Op. 6, No. 1, “Motto by C. W.” (1837)

clara-wieck-mazurka--schumann-davidsbund.claim: Clara Wieck and Schumann became secretly engaged on 14 August 1837, against her father’s opposition; within a week he began the Davidsbündlertänze. The opening bars, headed “Motto by C. W.”, quote the start of the mazurka that is No. 5 of her Soirées musicales, Op. 6, and he began to sketch a whole piece on her theme. Schumann later said that these pieces were more urgently addressed to her than anything else he had written; the published set is inscribed to Walther von Goethe, the poet’s grandson.

Her playing of Beethoven’s Appassionata moved the poet Franz Grillparzer to write “Clara Wieck und Beethoven” in January 1838. Schumann called it the most beautiful poem ever written about her and printed it in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik that month.

works.to: Schumann, Kreisleriana, Op. 16 (1838)

hoffmann-kreisler--schumann-kreisleriana.claim: Schumann’s eight Kreisleriana take their title from Johannes Kreisler, the eccentric, wild and witty Kapellmeister in E. T. A. Hoffmann’s Fantasy Pieces in Callot’s Manner and in Kater Murr. Schumann told Clara in 1838 that she and one of her ideas played the main role in the work, and that he wanted to dedicate it to her alone; the printed dedication is to Chopin. He said he wrote it in four days in April 1838, a claim one biographer dates differently, to between May and September.

works.to: Roméo et Juliette, Op. 17 (first given 24 November 1839)

Two days later he wrote that with Beethoven dead only Berlioz could revive him, and sent 20,000 francs through the Baron de Rothschild. The money cleared Berlioz’s debts and left him free to compose: Roméo et Juliette was given three times, on 24 November, 1 and 15 December 1839.

works.to: Chopin, 24 Préludes, Op. 28 (1835–39; published 1839)

He ordered them differently from Bach, by the circle of fifths with each major key followed by its relative minor, and wrote no fugues. Jean-Jacques Eigeldinger’s study of Chopin’s markings in the WTC copy of his pupil Pauline Chazaren shows that by 1838 he knew a Paris edition of the work thoroughly.

In May 1841 Wagner published an article that had a great deal to say about Berlioz, and in early 1860 he sent Berlioz the score of Tristan inscribed to “the dear and great author of Romeo and Juliet”, from “the grateful author of Tristan”. The editor of the Berlioz website takes the inscription as Wagner’s open acknowledgement of Berlioz’s influence on his work.

schubert-great-c-major--schumann-vienna-.claim: The Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde in Vienna, to whom Schubert had sent the score, tried it briefly and rejected it for its length and difficulty. In January 1839 Schumann visited Schubert’s brother Ferdinand in Vienna and discovered a copy of the manuscript among the composer’s papers; he took a copy back to Leipzig and sent it to Mendelssohn, who conducted the first complete public performance with the Gewandhaus Orchestra on 21 March 1839. Schumann’s article in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik praised the symphony’s “heavenly length”, likening it to a four-volume novel, perhaps by Jean Paul.

mickiewicz-ballades--chopin-ballade-1.title: Did Mickiewicz’s poems inspire Chopin’s Ballades?

works.from: Adam Mickiewicz, Ballady i romanse (1822) and Konrad Wallenrod (1828)
works.to: Chopin, Ballades Nos. 1–4 (No. 1, Op. 23, composed 1835–36)

mickiewicz-ballades--chopin-ballade-1.claim: In 1841 Robert Schumann reported in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik that Chopin had told him poems by the Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz inspired his ballades. Chopin left no statement of his own, and Schumann’s remark concerned the second Ballade in particular. A tradition links the first Ballade with Konrad Wallenrod, a poem about a Lithuanian raised among the Teutonic Knights who leads them to defeat; no document ties either piece to a particular poem. When Schumann visited Leipzig in 1836 he told Chopin that the G minor Ballade was his favourite of Chopin’s works, and Chopin replied that it was his too.
mickiewicz-ballades--chopin-ballade-1.note: Schumann’s 1841 report that Mickiewicz inspired the Ballades is documented; Chopin never named a poem, Schumann’s remark was “far from specific”, and the match of Ballade No. 1 with Konrad Wallenrod is a later tradition. Which poems, if any, stand behind which Ballade is unresolved.

They then reworked it together: the music was written on tinted paper, Wilhelm drew a vignette into the score for each month, and each piece carries a short poem by a German poet. It was through Mendelssohn that Berlioz was invited to Leipzig in 1843, where he gave Gewandhaus concerts on 4 and 22 February. The two exchanged batons “as a token of friendship”, but Berlioz noted that Mendelssohn praised his romances and said nothing of the symphonies, overtures or Requiem.

works.from: Bach, third subject of the unfinished fugue of The Art of Fugue (B♭–A–C–B♮)
works.to: Schumann, Six Fugues on the name BACH, Op. 60 (organ or pedal piano), 1845

bach-art-of-fugue--schumann-bach-fugues-.claim: Both Schumann and Liszt wrote works on the four-note motif that spells Bach’s name in German notation, and both helped found the Bach-Gesellschaft in 1850. Schumann finished his Six Fugues on the name BACH in November 1845, calling them the work that would, he believed, outlive his others, and saying he had tried to make them worthy of the great name they bear. The first fugue introduces the four notes slowly and builds from a sombre exposition; the second compresses the subject and adds Baroque semiquaver figures.

works.to: Wagner’s Dresden performance, Palm Sunday, 5 April 1846; Bayreuth foundation-stone concert, 1872

beethoven-9--wagner-dresden-palm-sunday-.claim: Wagner made a piano transcription of Beethoven’s Ninth in 1830, aged seventeen. On Palm Sunday, 5 April 1846, he conducted it in Dresden, where Robert Schumann was living and, on Christopher Reynolds’s evidence, also studying the work: both composers took from it a more contrapuntal, motivic style, and Reynolds points to Beethoven’s gradual build-up of the “Ode to Joy” melody. Wagner conducted the Ninth again to inaugurate the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, whose foundation stone was laid on 22 May 1872.

shakespeare-macbeth--verdi-macbeth-1847.title: Verdi sets Macbeth, his first Shakespeare opera

shakespeare-macbeth--verdi-macbeth-1847.claim: Verdi’s Macbeth, first given at the Teatro della Pergola in Florence on 14 March 1847, was the first Shakespeare play he adapted for the stage. He told his librettist Piave that the tragedy was “one of the greatest creations of man” and that if they could not make something great of it they should at least make something out of the ordinary. In 1865 he wrote that Shakespeare was “one of my favorite poets”, whom he had had “in my hands from my earliest youth”. For the revised version, given in French in Paris on 21 April 1865, he insisted that the Witches rule the drama.

berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.title: From Berlioz’s Witches’ Sabbath to Liszt’s Totentanz

works.from: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, V: Dies irae from bar 127, bassoons and ophicleides (1830)
works.to: Liszt, Totentanz: Paraphrase on Dies irae, S. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849)

berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.claim: In the finale of the Symphonie fantastique, Berlioz gives the Dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in C minor from bar 127, a funeral rite turned into a parody at the witches’ sabbath. Liszt met Berlioz the day before the premiere on 5 December 1830 and in 1833 made the piano transcription of the symphony. His Totentanz, planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859, is a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant. A second recorded source is the Triumph of Death fresco in the Campo Santo at Pisa, which Liszt saw in 1838.
berlioz-fantastique-dies-irae--liszt-tot.note: Both works are documented; no letter or statement has been found in which Liszt names the Fantastique as the source of the Dies irae idea. He knew the symphony intimately, but the Pisa fresco is the other recorded stimulus for the Totentanz.

works.from: Liszt’s Weimar production, Court Theatre, 28 August 1850
works.to: Wagner, Lohengrin, WWV 75

liszt-weimar--wagner-lohengrin-premiere-.claim: Wagner had fled Saxony after the May 1849 uprising in Dresden, in which he took part, and could not attend the first production of Lohengrin. Liszt conducted it at Weimar on 28 August 1850, a date he chose to honour Goethe, who was born there in 1749; David Trippett’s study calls the decision politically as well as artistically risky for the Weimar court. Wagner did not see a complete performance until Vienna in 1861; in the meantime he conducted extracts in Zürich, London, Paris and Brussels.

His biographer Mary Jane Phillips-Matz reports that he began composing at once, though Julian Budden notes that Verdi had probably read the book earlier. Francesco Maria Piave wrote the libretto, and La traviata was first performed at La Fenice, Venice, on 6 March 1853.

liszt-b-minor-sonata--brahms-weimar-1853.title: Did Brahms fall asleep during Liszt’s B minor Sonata?

works.to: Brahms’s visit to Weimar with Ede Reményi, June 1853

liszt-b-minor-sonata--brahms-weimar-1853.claim: In 1853 Brahms and the violinist Ede Reményi visited Weimar, where Brahms met Liszt, Peter Cornelius and Joachim Raff, and Liszt played Brahms’s Scherzo, Op. 4, at sight. Reményi later claimed that Brahms then slept while Liszt played his own B minor Sonata. This and other disagreements led Reményi and Brahms to part company; that autumn Brahms went instead to the Schumanns in Düsseldorf.
liszt-b-minor-sonata--brahms-weimar-1853.note: The only source for Brahms sleeping through the Sonata is Reményi’s account, written long afterwards and given by Brahms’s biographers as a claim. Liszt’s sight-reading of the Scherzo and the Weimar meetings are recorded; the Sonata was dedicated to Schumann and published only in 1854.

Robert is said to have broken off to fetch Clara, saying she must hear music “as you have never heard it before”; she noted in her diary that the visitor seemed “specially sent by God”. On 28 October Schumann published “Neue Bahnen” in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, naming Brahms as the one fated to give the age its highest and most ideal expression; publishers began to take an interest at once.

works.from: Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1819; 2nd ed. 1844)

schopenhauer--wagner-letter-to-liszt-185.claim: On 16 December 1854 Wagner wrote from Zürich to Liszt that he had been absorbed in a “gift from heaven”, Arthur Schopenhauer, “the greatest philosopher since Kant”; the poet Georg Herwegh had urged him to read The World as Will and Representation. In the same letter he announces Tristan und Isolde: never having known the true bliss of love, he would “erect a monument to the most beautiful of all my dreams”, a conception he calls the simplest but most full-blooded imaginable, ending under a black flag. The first musical sketches date from 19 December 1856, and on 9 August 1857 he broke off Siegfried to compose it.

works.to: The 1860 manifesto, almost certainly drafted by Brahms; Brahms’s help with Wagner’s concerts

wagner-new-german-school--brahms-manifes.claim: In 1860 a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik circulated with the signatures of Brahms, Joseph Joachim and others; its author was almost certainly Brahms. It leaked, the Neue Zeitschrift parodied it on 4 May, and it appeared in the Echo on 6 May with more than twenty names. Yet in Vienna Brahms helped prepare Wagner’s concerts of 1862–63, was given a manuscript of part of Tannhäuser (Wagner demanded it back in 1875), and in January 1863 played Wagner his Handel Variations; the meeting was cordial.

wagner-tristan-prelude--berlioz-debats-1.title: Berlioz “reads and re-reads” the Tristan prelude, baffled

works.from: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde, Act I prelude (concert at the Salle Ventadour, February 1860)
works.to: Berlioz, review of Wagner’s concerts, Journal des Débats, 9 February 1860

wagner-tristan-prelude--berlioz-debats-1.claim: Wagner’s Paris concerts of January–February 1860 included the Tristan prelude, and Berlioz reviewed them in the Journal des Débats on 9 February. He describes a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. He says he has read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still cannot tell what the composer means. Wagner, who had sent him the Tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 February.

He wrote the work in a single stretch in September 1861, twenty-five variations and a fugue, and gave it to Schumann on her forty-second birthday, 13 September. berlioz-treatise--rimsky-korsakov-orches.claim: Inexperienced in orchestration when he began his First Symphony in 1861, Rimsky-Korsakov turned to Hector Berlioz’s treatise as well as to the advice of Balakirev. Thirty years later, in the 1891 preface to his own Principles of Orchestration, he named Berlioz first among the colourists, with Glinka, Liszt and Wagner, who had brought orchestral colour to its zenith. He told students that Weber, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Glinka, Wagner, Liszt and modern French and Russian composers would be their best guides.

hanslick--wagner-beckmesser-1862.title: Wagner’s Beckmesser began as “Veit Hanslich”

works.from: Eduard Hanslick, Vienna’s leading critic (On the Musically Beautiful, 1854)
works.to: Wagner, Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg: the Merker, then Beckmesser (prose draft 1861; reading in Vienna, 23 November 1862)

hanslick--wagner-beckmesser-1862.claim: When Wagner turned the Meistersinger prose draft into a libretto in Vienna in 1861, he named the pedantic town clerk who marks the singers’ faults “Veit Hanslich”, an open allusion to the Vienna critic Eduard Hanslick. By the time Wagner first read the text aloud in Vienna on 23 November 1862, with Hanslick among the listeners, the name had become Sixtus Beckmesser. Hanslick, who championed Schumann and Brahms against Wagner and Liszt, knew he was the target.
hanslick--wagner-beckmesser-1862.note: The draft name “Veit Hanslich” and Hanslick’s presence at the 1862 reading are documented; that the finished Beckmesser caricatures Hanslick is an interpretation, and general reference works still say only that it is “sometimes claimed”.

wagner-st-petersburg--tchaikovsky-concer.title: Tchaikovsky attends all six Wagner concerts in St Petersburg

works.from: Wagner conducting in St Petersburg, 1863: Tristan prelude and Liebestod, Beethoven symphonies and others
works.to: Tchaikovsky’s Bayreuth reports of 1876 and his later verdict on Wagner

wagner-st-petersburg--tchaikovsky-concer.claim: In 1863, in his first year at the Conservatory, Tchaikovsky attended all six concerts that Wagner gave in St Petersburg. They included the Prelude and “Liebestod” from Tristan und Isolde and Beethoven’s Third and Fifth to Eighth symphonies; Tchaikovsky counted the experience among the most memorable of his life. In 1875 he heard Klindworth play through the whole Ring in piano transcription, and in August 1876 he reached Bayreuth for the first Rheingold as correspondent for a Moscow newspaper.

works.from: Balakirev’s guidance of the young naval cadet, 1861–65
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Symphony No. 1, Op. 1 (premiered by Balakirev, December 1865)

balakirev-lessons--rimsky-korsakov-symph.claim: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote his Symphony No. 1 between 1861 and 1865 under the guidance of Balakirev, who conducted its first performance at a Free Music School concert in December 1865. The composer acknowledged Schumann’s Manfred Overture and Third Symphony, Glinka’s Prince Kholmsky and Balakirev’s King Lear overture as models. He later wrote that he felt his own ignorance but was convinced that Balakirev knew everything, and that Balakirev cleverly concealed from him and the others of “The Five” the insufficiency of his own training.

dargomyzhsky-stone-guest--mussorgsky-mar.title: Mussorgsky sets Gogol’s Marriage as Dargomyzhsky set Pushkin

works.from: Dargomyzhsky, The Stone Guest, Pushkin’s text set “just as it stands” (begun 1866)
works.to: Mussorgsky, Zhenitba (Marriage), after Gogol’s comedy (begun 1868; unfinished)

dargomyzhsky-stone-guest--mussorgsky-mar.claim: Mussorgsky’s idea of setting Gogol’s comedy Marriage came from the advice and example of Alexander Dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began The Stone Guest, declaring that Pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. It replaced the division between aria and recitative with a continuous, syllabic but lyrically heightened declamation. In 1868 Mussorgsky quickly set the first eleven scenes of Gogol’s prose, catching the natural accents of its humdrum dialogue; he left the work unfinished.

pushkin-boris-godunov--mussorgsky-boris-.title: Mussorgsky turns Pushkin’s Boris Godunov into an opera

works.from: Pushkin, Boris Godunov (written 1825, published 1831); Karamzin, History of the Russian State
works.to: Mussorgsky, Boris Godunov (original version 1869; revised 1872; premiere 27 January 1874)

pushkin-boris-godunov--mussorgsky-boris-.claim: In the autumn of 1868 the historian Vladimir Nikolsky suggested to Mussorgsky an opera on Pushkin’s “dramatic chronicle” Boris Godunov, and Lyudmila Shestakova gave him a volume of Pushkin’s plays interleaved with blank pages; he began his own libretto in October. He finished the score in December 1869, and the Imperial Theatres rejected it on 10 February 1871 by six votes to one, ostensibly for lack of a major female role. The revised version of 1872 was first performed at the Mariinsky Theatre on 27 January 1874.

balakirev-fantasy--tchaikovsky-romeo-and.title: Balakirev sets Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet in order

works.from: Balakirev’s letters and his overture King Lear (as formal model), 1869
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Romeo and Juliet, fantasy overture (first version 1869; dedicated to Balakirev)

balakirev-fantasy--tchaikovsky-romeo-and.claim: Balakirev suggested the subject of Romeo and Juliet to Tchaikovsky when they met in Moscow in the summer of 1869, after criticising Tchaikovsky’s Fatum frankly. He sent a plan describing the type of music for each section, with advice on keys, and held up his own King Lear overture as a model. Tchaikovsky wrote on 14 October 1869 that he was “played out completely”; “abusive letters” from Balakirev followed, and on 24 October he reported he was writing the overture. The work is dedicated to Balakirev, though the inscription was left off the first printed scores.

wagner-lohengrin--verdi-bologna-1871.title: Verdi annotates Lohengrin at Bologna, November 1871

works.from: Wagner, Lohengrin, Italian premiere at the Teatro Comunale, Bologna, 1 November 1871
works.to: Verdi’s pencilled notes in a vocal score, 9 November 1871

wagner-lohengrin--verdi-bologna-1871.claim: Angelo Mariani conducted the first performance of a Wagner opera in Italy, Lohengrin at the Teatro Comunale of Bologna, on 1 November 1871. On 9 November Verdi attended and annotated a copy of the vocal score with his impressions and opinions; it was almost certainly his first exposure to Wagner’s music. In 1887 a German visitor recorded him as saying there was much to admire in Tannhäuser and Lohengrin, but that in his later operas Wagner seemed to overstep the limits of what music can express.

wagner-tannhauser--bruckner-symphony-3-1.title: Bruckner dedicates his Third Symphony to Wagner

works.from: Wagner, Die Walküre, Tristan und Isolde, Lohengrin, Tannhäuser
works.to: Bruckner, Symphony No. 3 in D minor, WAB 103 (1873 version)

wagner-tannhauser--bruckner-symphony-3-1.claim: In September 1873, before the Third Symphony was finished, Bruckner visited Wagner, whom he had first met at the Munich premiere of Tristan und Isolde in 1865. He showed Wagner his Second and Third Symphonies and asked him to choose; Wagner chose the Third, and Bruckner dedicated it to him. The 1873 score quoted Wagner’s Die Walküre and Tristan in the first movement and Lohengrin and Walküre in the Adagio; after the Vienna premiere of 1877 failed, Bruckner’s revisions removed most of these quotations.

works.from: Viktor Hartmann’s drawings and designs, memorial exhibition, St Petersburg, February–March 1874
works.to: Mussorgsky, Pictures at an Exhibition, piano suite (composed 2–22 June 1874)

hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1.claim: Viktor Hartmann, an architect and designer, died suddenly on 4 August 1873, aged thirty-nine. The critic Vladimir Stasov helped organise a memorial exhibition of over 400 of his works at the Imperial Academy of Arts in February and March 1874; Mussorgsky lent the two pictures Hartmann had given him in 1868 and viewed the show. He composed Pictures at an Exhibition between 2 and 22 June 1874 and dedicated it to Stasov. “Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks” answers Hartmann’s costume sketch of canary chicks for the ballet Trilby (1871).

works.from: Beethoven, Symphony No. 9, finale: “Ode to Joy” theme (1824)
works.to: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, finale: main Allegro theme (first performed 4 November 1876)

beethoven-9-finale--brahms-1-finale-them.claim: The broad tune that Brahms gives the strings in the C-major Allegro of his First Symphony finale resembles the “Ode to Joy” theme of Beethoven’s Ninth. When this was pointed out to him he is reported to have answered “Any ass can see that”. In 1877 the conductor Hans von Bülow called the symphony “Beethoven’s Tenth”; it was first played at Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876 under Felix Otto Dessoff.

works.to: Puccini’s career in the opera house

verdi--puccini-aida-pisa.claim: In 1876, aged eighteen, Puccini walked about twenty kilometres from Lucca to Pisa to hear the first local performance of Verdi’s Aida. He said later that when he heard it in Pisa he felt “a musical window had opened for me”, and the experience is credited with turning him from church music towards the theatre.

pushkin-onegin--tchaikovsky-onegin-1877.title: Tchaikovsky sets Pushkin’s own verses in Eugene Onegin

works.from: Pushkin, Eugene Onegin, verse novel (1825–32)
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Eugene Onegin, “lyrical scenes”, Op. 24 (premiere 29 March 1879)

pushkin-onegin--tchaikovsky-onegin-1877.claim: In May 1877 the singer Yelizaveta Lavrovskaya proposed to Tchaikovsky an opera on Pushkin’s verse novel. He doubted the plot was strong enough, but after a sleepless night embraced the idea and drafted the scenario in a single night. With Konstantin Shilovsky’s minor help he used original verses from Pushkin and chose scenes from the characters’ emotional lives, calling the work “lyrical scenes”. It was first performed at the Maly Theatre in Moscow on 29 March 1879.

brahms-hungarian-dances--dvorak-slavonic.title: Brahms recommends Dvořák to Simrock; Slavonic Dances follow

works.from: Brahms, Hungarian Dances (piano four hands) and his referral to Simrock
works.to: Dvořák, Slavonic Dances, Op. 46 (1878; orchestrated for Simrock)

brahms-hungarian-dances--dvorak-slavonic.claim: Dvořák won the Austrian State Prize in 1874, 1876 and 1877. Brahms, on the committee, referred him to his own publisher, Fritz Simrock, who first issued the Moravian Duets and then asked for something dance-like. Unsure how to begin, Dvořák took Brahms’s Hungarian Dances as a model, but only as a model: Brahms used real Hungarian folk melodies, whereas Dvořák mostly used the characteristic rhythms of Bohemian folk dances with melodies of his own. The Op. 46 set, written for piano four hands, was orchestrated soon after at Simrock’s request.

works.from: Symphony No. 3, 1877 version

bruckner--mahler-third-piano-duet.claim: Mahler and Rudolf Krzyzanowski prepared a piano-duet arrangement of Bruckner’s Third Symphony. Reducing the orchestral work to four hands was practical, detailed engagement with Bruckner’s construction, not merely admiration from a distance; the precise division of work between the two arrangers should not be treated as settled.

wagner--mahler-parsifal-bayreuth.claim: Mahler heard Parsifal at Bayreuth in 1883 under Hermann Levi and reported the experience to Fritz Löhr. bach-bwv150--brahms-4-finale-passacaglia.title: Brahms’s Fourth ends on Bach’s Cantata 150 bass

works.from: Bach, Cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich, BWV 150, closing chaconne
works.to: Brahms, Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98, finale: passacaglia

bach-bwv150--brahms-4-finale-passacaglia.claim: The finale of Brahms’s Fourth Symphony is a passacaglia on an eight-bar theme adapted from the closing chaconne of Bach’s Cantata 150, which was then unpublished. Brahms added a leading tone to Bach’s bass and regularised its rhythm into eight dotted half notes that rise from the tonic E to the dominant B, drop an octave and return. The theme is stated thirty times, always eight bars long, before the coda begins at bar 253.

works.from: Nikolai Zverev’s residential piano teaching
works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow training, from 1885

zverev--rachmaninoff-moscow-household.claim: Rachmaninoff entered Nikolai Zverev’s Moscow household as a piano pupil in 1885. Its musical gatherings also brought him into contact with Tchaikovsky, so the teacher provided both intensive pianistic training and access to the professional circle in which the young composer was first heard.

mussorgsky-bald-mountain--rimsky-korsako.title: Rimsky-Korsakov rebuilds Mussorgsky’s Bald Mountain in 1886

works.from: Mussorgsky, St John’s Eve on Bald Mountain (1867); Mlada (1872); The Fair at Sorochyntsi (1880)
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Night on Bald Mountain (completed and published 1886)

mussorgsky-bald-mountain--rimsky-korsako.claim: Mussorgsky finished St John’s Eve on Bald Mountain on 23 June 1867, but Balakirev refused to perform it, so he reused the music in the collaborative opera-ballet Mlada (1872) and in The Fair at Sorochyntsi (1880). After Mussorgsky’s death in 1881 Rimsky-Korsakov made his own version, completed and published in 1886, and wrote that its form, modulations and orchestration had resisted him for two years. He conducted the first performance at the Russian Symphony Concerts in St Petersburg on 15 October 1886 and made substantial “corrections” to melody, harmony, rhythm and dynamics.

mozart-don-giovanni--tchaikovsky-mozarti.title: Tchaikovsky orchestrates Mozart piano pieces as Mozartiana

works.from: Mozart: Gigue, K. 574; Minuet, K. 355; Liszt’s transcription of Ave verum corpus; variations on a theme of Gluck
works.to: Tchaikovsky, Suite No. 4 “Mozartiana”, Op. 61 (June–July 1887)

mozart-don-giovanni--tchaikovsky-mozarti.claim: Tchaikovsky told his diary in 1886 that he loved Beethoven as one fears God but loved Mozart “as a musical Christ”. At sixteen or seventeen he had heard Don Giovanni almost by chance and called it a revelation; on 17 May 1884 he wrote “Played Mozart and was in raptures. Thought about a suite from Mozart.” In June and July 1887 he orchestrated four pieces, among them the Gigue, K. 574, and the Minuet, K. 355, as the Suite No. 4, which he described to his publisher as “the old given a contemporary treatment”.

arabian-nights--rimsky-korsakov-schehera.title: Rimsky-Korsakov takes Scheherazade from the Thousand and One Nights

works.from: The Thousand and One Nights; the story of Prince Ajib
works.to: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, Op. 35 (1888; premiere 28 October 1888)

arabian-nights--rimsky-korsakov-schehera.claim: Rimsky-Korsakov composed Scheherazade in 1888 on themes from the Thousand and One Nights. After weighing the opinions of Anatoly Lyadov and others, and his own dislike of a too-definite programme, he settled on thematic headings such as “The Young Prince and the Young Princess”, deliberately vague, though the finale’s epigraph does refer to the adventure of Prince Ajib. In a later edition he dropped the titles altogether, wanting listeners to hear oriental-flavoured symphonic music that suggests fairy-tale adventure.

works.from: The Requiem sequence Dies irae (Gregorian chant; setting tradition)
works.to: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48 (1887–90; first version 1888)

gregorian-chant--faure-requiem-dies-irae.claim: Fauré’s Requiem sets seven movements and omits the full sequence Dies irae, keeping only its closing section, the Pie Jesu; he followed a French Baroque tradition in this, did not set the Benedictus, and added two texts from the burial service, Libera me and In paradisum. He wrote that everything he could muster of religious illusion went into the work, which is “dominated from beginning to end by a very human feeling of faith in eternal rest”. hans-rott--mahler-symphonic-scherzos.title: Rott’s scherzo: resemblance is not proof

works.from: Symphony in E major, scherzo, 1878–1880
works.to: Symphony No. 1, scherzo; comparison with Symphony No. 5

hans-rott--mahler-symphonic-scherzos.claim: Hans Rott’s E-major Symphony contains Ländler-like scherzo writing that has been compared with Mahler’s First and Fifth Symphonies. Mahler knew Rott as a fellow student and later praised his music, but the securely reported loan of Rott’s score in 1900 comes after the First Symphony’s composition. Similarity, friendship and later possession of a score do not by themselves prove when Mahler first knew that passage or that he copied it.

This pianistic relationship ran alongside, rather than replaced, the separate composition and counterpoint instruction he received from Arensky and Taneyev.

works.to: Fauré and Messager, Souvenirs de Bayreuth, quadrille for piano four hands (c. 1888; published 1930)

wagner-ring--faure-souvenirs-de-bayreuth.claim: From 1878 Fauré and his former pupil André Messager travelled to hear Wagner: Das Rheingold and Die Walküre at Cologne, the whole Ring at Munich and London, and Die Meistersinger and Parsifal at Bayreuth. Their joint Souvenirs de Bayreuth, a “fantasy in the form of a quadrille on favourite themes from the Ring”, was composed probably in 1888 and published in 1930. It grew from improvisations at Marguerite de Saint-Marceaux’s salon, which Colette recalled; Fauré admired Wagner yet is described as one of the few of his generation to escape his musical influence.

larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.title: A rune singer teaches Sibelius how Finnish sings

works.from: Larin Paraske’s rune singing, Porvoo (1891)
works.to: Kullervo, Op. 7 (1892)

larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.claim: At the end of 1891 Sibelius travelled with the aesthetician Yrjö Hirn to Porvoo to hear the Izhorian rune singer Larin Paraske. Sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses Finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. Kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the Kalevala, followed in 1892.
larin-paraske--sibelius-kullervo.note: Hirn’s recollection and Sibelius’s own account place a hearing at Porvoo at the end of 1891, while Sibelius later claimed he first met Paraske on his 1892 honeymoon in Lieksa. That he heard her is documented; where and when he first did is not settled, and how far her singing shaped Kullervo is interpretation.

hoffmann-nutcracker--tchaikovsky-ballet-.title: Hoffmann’s Nutcracker reaches Tchaikovsky through Dumas

works.from: E. T. A. Hoffmann, Nussknacker und Mausekönig (1816), in Dumas’s Histoire d’un casse-noisette (1845)
works.to: Tchaikovsky, The Nutcracker, Op. 71 (February 1891–April 1892)

hoffmann-nutcracker--tchaikovsky-ballet-.claim: The libretto of Tchaikovsky’s last ballet was compiled by Ivan Vsevolozhsky and Marius Petipa from Alexandre Dumas’s Histoire d’un Casse-Noisette (1845), which Dumas adapted from E. T. A. Hoffmann’s Der Nußknacker und Mausekönig (1816). Tchaikovsky wrote and orchestrated the score between February 1891 and April 1892, and drew a concert suite of eight numbers from it. The Christmas Eve setting is in eighteenth-century Germany, in the home of President Silberhaus.

peladan--satie-sonneries.title: Péladan makes Satie composer to the Rose+Croix

works.from: Salon de la Rose+Croix, Paris (10 March–10 April 1892)
works.to: Sonneries de la Rose+Croix (1892)

peladan--satie-sonneries.claim: Sâr Joséphin Péladan, founder of the Ordre de la Rose-Croix Catholique, invited Satie to become the order’s official composer. For Péladan’s first Salon de la Rose-Croix (10 March–10 April 1892), each gathering opened with a Solemn Mass of the Holy Ghost, preceded by three fanfares for harp and trumpet that Satie composed. They were published as Sonneries de la Rose+Croix, music written for the order’s ceremonies rather than the concert hall.

sources.title: Interlude: Erik Satie, The Rosicrucian Adventure

burleigh-spirituals--dvorak-new-world-18.title: Burleigh sings spirituals to Dvořák in New York

works.from: Spirituals sung by Harry T. Burleigh at the National Conservatory, New York
works.to: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9 “From the New World”, Largo (premiere 16 December 1893)

burleigh-spirituals--dvorak-new-world-18.claim: While Dvořák directed the National Conservatory in New York, the African-American student Harry T. Burleigh sang traditional spirituals to him; Burleigh said Dvořák absorbed their “spirit” before writing his own melodies. Dvořák is said to have given the Largo’s main theme to the cor anglais rather than the clarinet because it reminded him of Burleigh’s voice. In the New York Herald of 1893 he said the future music of America must be founded on what are called Negro melodies. The first movement’s closing theme resembles “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot”, but Dvořák wrote his own themes.
burleigh-spirituals--dvorak-new-world-18.note: Burleigh’s role as singer and Dvořák’s published statements about Negro melodies are documented; the cor anglais anecdote is reported as hearsay (“was said to have”), and Dvořák denied quoting existing tunes, so the resemblance to “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot” remains an observation, not a documented borrowing.

sources.title: Symphony No. 9 (Dvořák) (Wikipedia): Largo; Influences; the New York Herald statements

chabrier--ravel-serenade-grotesque.title: Chabrier behind the grotesque serenade

works.from: Chabrier’s piano music
works.to: Sérénade grotesque

chabrier--ravel-serenade-grotesque.claim: In his autobiographical account, Ravel explicitly associated his early Sérénade grotesque with Chabrier’s influence. This is the composer identifying a model for a particular piece, a stronger connection than a later critic hearing a general family likeness between two French piano styles.

sources.title: Peter Jost / Henle: Between distance and admiration: Satie and Ravel

jean-paul--mahler-titan-title.title: Titan was a title, not a plot

works.from: Titan, novel
works.to: Symphony No. 1: Hamburg programme, 1893

jean-paul--mahler-titan-title.claim: Mahler attached the name Titan, borrowed from Jean Paul’s novel, to the First Symphony for its Hamburg performance in 1893. The title does not establish a movement-by-movement setting of the novel: Mahler subsequently withdrew the programme and title, leaving a four-movement symphony.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 1, introduction
sources.locator: Hamburg 1893 and withdrawal of the programme

longfellow-hiawatha--dvorak-new-world-18.title: Dvořák calls the Largo a Hiawatha study

works.from: Longfellow, The Song of Hiawatha (1855)
works.to: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, Largo and Scherzo

longfellow-hiawatha--dvorak-new-world-18.claim: In the New York Herald of 15 December 1893, the day before the premiere at Carnegie Hall, Dvořák said that he regarded the second movement as a “sketch or study” for a later cantata or opera on Longfellow’s Hiawatha, and that the Scherzo was suggested by the scene of the feast where the Indians dance. No such cantata or opera was written. The symphony was commissioned by the New York Philharmonic and first played on 16 December 1893 under Anton Seidl.

sources.title: Symphony No. 9 (Dvořák) (Wikipedia): the Herald article of 15 December 1893

satie--ravel-ballade-reine.title: Ravel names Satie as an early model

works.from: Satie’s early music
works.to: Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer

satie--ravel-ballade-reine.claim: Ravel’s autobiographical sketch names Satie as an influence on the early Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer. The piece is not available for a reliable musical comparison, so the evidence here is Ravel’s own retrospective statement rather than a reconstructed passage or an invented quotation.

sources.locator: Ravel’s autobiographical sketch and the Ballade

tchaikovsky--rachmaninoff-aleko-patronag.title: Tchaikovsky champions the graduation opera

works.from: Tchaikovsky’s support and proposed Iolanta double bill
works.to: Aleko, composed 1892; Bolshoi premiere, 1893

tchaikovsky--rachmaninoff-aleko-patronag.claim: Tchaikovsky publicly praised Rachmaninoff’s graduation opera Aleko, attended its Bolshoi premiere in 1893 and proposed pairing it with his own Iolanta. This was concrete patronage of a younger composer’s work, not simply a later listener’s comparison of their melodies.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: December 1892 interview; Aleko premiere, 27 April/9 May 1893; Iolanta proposal

tchaikovsky--rachmaninoff-elegiac-trio.title: A memorial trio answers a memorial trio

works.from: Piano Trio in A minor, Op. 50, in memory of Nikolai Rubinstein
works.to: Trio élégiaque No. 2 in D minor, Op. 9

tchaikovsky--rachmaninoff-elegiac-trio.claim: After Tchaikovsky’s death, Rachmaninoff composed his Second Trio élégiaque in his memory, completing it in December 1893. The choice of a large piano trio as a memorial follows the precedent of Tchaikovsky’s own trio for Nikolai Rubinstein: the younger composer mourned his patron in a form that patron had already made commemorative.

wunderhorn--mahler-fish-sermon.title: The fish sermon loses its words

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt
works.to: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt; Symphony No. 2, movement III

wunderhorn--mahler-fish-sermon.claim: In Mahler’s Wunderhorn song, Saint Anthony preaches to attentive fish who return unchanged to their usual behaviour. Its musical material also supplies the Second Symphony’s instrumental scherzo, so the poem’s circular, unsuccessful sermon has an afterlife without a singer to explain it.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction

wunderhorn--mahler-urlicht.title: A folk poem interrupts the symphony

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Urlicht
works.to: Urlicht; Symphony No. 2, movement IV

wunderhorn--mahler-urlicht.claim: Mahler set Urlicht, a poem from the folk-poetry anthology Des Knaben Wunderhorn, before placing it between the Second Symphony’s scherzo and finale. The alto’s intimate appeal for release is a new vocal presence after three instrumental movements: the borrowed material is the poem, not a documented traditional tune.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
Mahler Foundation: Urlicht

klopstock--mahler-resurrection-finale.title: A memorial service unlocks the finale

works.from: Die Auferstehung
works.to: Symphony No. 2, finale

klopstock--mahler-resurrection-finale.claim: At the memorial service for Hans von Bülow in 1894, Mahler heard Klopstock’s resurrection hymn and found the textual starting point for his Second Symphony’s finale. He did not simply set the complete hymn: his finale joins part of Klopstock’s poem to verses of his own.

mallarme--debussy-faune.title: Mallarmé’s faun finds its music

works.from: L’après-midi d’un faune (poem, 1876)
works.to: Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune (1894)

mallarme--debussy-faune.claim: Debussy’s orchestral prelude, first performed in Paris on 22 December 1894 under Gustave Doret, takes Mallarmé’s poem as its subject; Debussy called it “a very free illustration” of the poem, not a synthesis of it. Mallarmé had doubted that music should be set beside poetry, but after attending the premiere at Debussy’s invitation he wrote that the music went further than his text “into nostalgia and into light”.

bach--mahler-hamburg-score-study.title: Bach on the composing-hut desk

works.from: Bach-Gesellschaft collected edition; contrapuntal works
works.to: Mahler’s Bach study during the Hamburg years

bach--mahler-hamburg-score-study.claim: Records of the Bach-Gesellschaft edition place Mahler among its subscribers during his Hamburg years, and recollections by Natalie Bauer-Lechner and Alma Mahler describe his sustained study of Bach. The report that Bach scores accompanied him to his composing retreat makes this a working relationship with counterpoint, not merely a name on a list of favourite composers.

chopin--scriabin-preludes-op-11.title: Scriabin’s 24 Preludes follow Chopin’s plan

works.from: Chopin, 24 Preludes, Op. 28 (1839)
works.to: Scriabin, 24 Preludes, Op. 11 (1888–96)

chopin--scriabin-preludes-op-11.claim: Scriabin’s Op. 11 keeps strictly to the circle of fifths to cover every major and minor key, the plan of Chopin’s Op. 28 set. Both cycles are built alike, with pieces arranged in relative major and minor pairs, and the resemblance sits beside a wider spiritual kinship with Chopin that runs through Scriabin’s early music.
chopin--scriabin-preludes-op-11.note: The sources describe the likeness of construction between the two cycles; a statement by Scriabin that he modelled Op. 11 on Op. 28 was not found.

nietzsche--mahler-third-midnight-song.title: Zarathustra sings at midnight

works.from: Also sprach Zarathustra: Midnight Song
works.to: Symphony No. 3, movement IV

nietzsche--mahler-third-midnight-song.claim: After three instrumental movements, the Third Symphony introduces an alto singing Nietzsche’s midnight poem from Also sprach Zarathustra. The sparse, slow setting changes the scale of listening from the preceding orchestral world to a single voice contemplating sorrow and eternity; this is an actual text setting, not a claim that the whole symphony illustrates Nietzsche’s philosophy.

nietzsche--richard-strauss-zarathustra.title: Strauss answers Nietzsche in a tone poem

works.from: Also sprach Zarathustra (1883–85)
works.to: Also sprach Zarathustra, Op. 30 (1896)

nietzsche--richard-strauss-zarathustra.claim: Strauss conducted the first performance of his tone poem in Frankfurt on 27 November 1896, and named its sections after chapters of Nietzsche’s book (“Of the Backworldsmen”, “Of the Great Longing”). Strauss insisted that he had not meant to write philosophical music or to portray Nietzsche’s work, but “to convey in music an idea of the evolution of the human race” up to Nietzsche’s idea of the Übermensch.

debussy--satie-gymnopedies-orchestrated.title: Debussy orchestrates two Gymnopédies

works.from: Debussy’s orchestration of Gymnopédies Nos. 3 and 1 (1897)
works.to: Gymnopédies (1888)

debussy--satie-gymnopedies-orchestrated.claim: In February 1897, when Satie’s popularity was waning and his finances deteriorating, Debussy orchestrated the third and first Gymnopédies to draw public attention to his friend’s music. When Debussy published the scores two years later he reversed the numbering, so that Satie’s first became his third. The two had met in 1890 and found each other kindred spirits in their experimental approach to composition.

works.from: Fauré’s Paris Conservatoire composition class
works.to: Ravel’s studies; early Sonata for violin and piano

faure--ravel-composition-class.claim: Ravel studied composition with Fauré from 1897, and his early single-movement violin sonata belongs to that classroom world. Bru Zane identifies a probable performance in Fauré’s class in 1897–1898 and hears the older composer’s chamber-music example in it; the classroom performance is reported as probable, not certain.

works.from: André Gédalge’s private counterpoint instruction
works.to: Ravel’s Conservatoire-period training

gedalge--ravel-counterpoint.claim: Alongside Fauré’s composition class, Ravel took private counterpoint lessons with André Gédalge. works.from: Piano Sonata No. 8, “Pathétique”, slow movement (1799)
works.to: Enigma Variations, Variation IX “Nimrod” (1899)

beethoven--elgar-nimrod-pathetique.claim: Elgar said Nimrod came from a day when he was ready to give up composing and his publisher August Jaeger urged him on, pointing to Beethoven, who wrote more and more beautiful music despite his worries, and singing the theme of the Pathétique sonata’s slow movement. Elgar told Dora Penny that the opening bars of Nimrod were made to suggest that theme: “Only a hint, not a quotation”.

works.from: Gymnopédies and early piano harmony
works.to: Pavane pour une infante défunte, original piano version

satie--ravel-pavane-harmonic-comparison.claim: Peter Jost compares the Pavane’s calmly sustained dissonances and unexpected bass support with Satie’s early piano writing. This is a harmonic comparison, not a claim that Ravel copied the Gymnopédie melody; the excerpt isolates Ravel’s tune so that the listener can distinguish melody from the accompaniment where the proposed resemblance lies.

works.from: Hymn tunes, town-band music, Stephen Foster
works.to: Ives’s songs, symphonies and sonatas

american-hymn-and-band--ives.claim: The sources of Ives’s tonal imagery included hymn tunes and traditional songs. He also incorporated the melodies of town bands at holiday parades, fiddlers at Saturday-night dances, patriotic songs, sentimental parlour ballads and the tunes of Stephen Foster.

dostoevsky--mahler-childhood-faith-readi.title: Reading the symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov

works.from: The Brothers Karamazov
works.to: Symphonies Nos. 3 and 4

dostoevsky--mahler-childhood-faith-readi.claim: Celeste Belknap’s study places Mahler’s Third and Fourth Symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov, a novel Mahler admired, especially around faith, nihilism and childhood. This offers a specific interpretative lens for the Fourth’s childlike heaven, not proof that Mahler secretly composed a Dostoevsky programme.
dostoevsky--mahler-childhood-faith-readi.note: Mahler’s admiration for Dostoevsky is distinct from Belknap’s proposed structural and philosophical parallels; a direct compositional dependence is not established.

newman--elgar-gerontius.title: Elgar sets Newman’s poem of a dying soul

works.from: The Dream of Gerontius (poem, 1865)
works.to: The Dream of Gerontius, Op. 38 (1900)

newman--elgar-gerontius.claim: Elgar had owned a copy of Newman’s poem since at least 1885, and in 1889 he was given another as a wedding present; that copy carried handwritten transcriptions of notes made by General Gordon. He thought of the text in musical terms for years before setting it for the Birmingham Triennial Festival, where The Dream of Gerontius was first performed on 3 October 1900.

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Das himmlische Leben
works.to: Symphony No. 4, finale

wunderhorn--mahler-heavenly-life.claim: Mahler composed Das himmlische Leben in 1892, well before the Fourth Symphony, and subsequently reorchestrated it for that work’s finale. The soprano describes a childlike heaven of food, saints and music; the apparently simple conclusion is therefore an older song around which a new symphonic destination was built.

works.from: Reinhold Glière’s summer composition teaching

works.from: Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20
works.to: Variations on a Theme of Chopin, Op. 22

works.from: Kindertotenlieder, poems written after the deaths of two children

ruckert--mahler-kindertotenlieder.claim: Friedrich Rückert wrote his Kindertotenlieder after losing two children in 1833–1834; Mahler selected five poems for his song cycle. works.from: Schoenberg’s teaching in Vienna (1904–11)
works.to: Berg’s early works, from the Piano Sonata, Op. 1

schoenberg--berg-lessons.claim: Berg studied counterpoint, music theory and harmony with Schoenberg between 1904 and 1911. He adopted his teacher’s principle of developing variation and, later, the twelve-tone technique, which shapes the Lyric Suite and the Violin Concerto.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Alban Berg

hokusai--debussy-la-mer-cover.title: Hokusai’s wave on the cover of La mer

works.from: The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1831)
works.to: La mer, first edition of the orchestral score (Durand, 1905)

hokusai--debussy-la-mer-cover.claim: The first edition of the orchestral score of La mer (Durand, 1905) carried a detail of Hokusai’s Great Wave off Kanagawa on its cover: roughly the left half of the print, the great wave with a smaller wave in front of it. The choice of the print is credited to Debussy and is read as a sign of how much Japanese art meant to him. What is documented is the cover; how far the picture shaped the music is a matter of interpretation.

goethe--mahler-eighth-faust.title: Faust answers Veni creator spiritus

works.from: Faust, Part II, closing scene
works.to: Symphony No. 8, Part II

goethe--mahler-eighth-faust.claim: The Eighth Symphony’s second part sets the closing scene of Goethe’s Faust II, following a first part built on the Latin hymn Veni creator spiritus. Mahler links these apparently distant texts through returning musical material, making Goethe’s final ascent the continuation of the opening invocation rather than a separate cantata appended to it.

hungarian-peasant-song--bartok-phonograp.title: Bartók records peasant songs on the phonograph

works.from: Peasant songs recorded in Békés County and elsewhere (1906–08)
works.to: Bartók’s folk-song collections and the music built on them

hungarian-peasant-song--bartok-phonograp.claim: Bartók’s first year of substantial folk-song collecting was 1906: that summer he used a phonograph on his first systematic trip, to Békés County, and over the year he collected more than a thousand Hungarian songs and some three hundred Slovak ones. In 1907–08 he went on to Felsőireg and to the Transylvanian regions of Csík and Gyergyó. Following Béla Vikár, he used the phonograph from the beginning to complete his written notes with sound recordings.

isaac--webern-choralis-constantinus.title: Webern edits Isaac and learns the interplay of parts

works.from: Choralis Constantinus II (early 16th century)
works.to: Webern’s doctoral edition and his later counterpoint

isaac--webern-choralis-constantinus.claim: For his musicology doctorate under Guido Adler, Webern edited the second part of Heinrich Isaac’s Choralis Constantinus. As a composer he would emulate its “subtle organization in the interplay of parts”, a discipline he carried from the study of Renaissance polyphony into his own writing.

lyadov--prokofiev-counterpoint.title: Lyadov’s rules meet an impatient modernist

works.from: Anatoly Lyadov’s harmony and counterpoint teaching
works.to: Prokofiev’s St Petersburg Conservatory studies

lyadov--prokofiev-counterpoint.claim: Prokofiev studied harmony and counterpoint with Anatoly Lyadov, whose teaching he found uninspiring. The publisher’s chronology records Lyadov’s alarm at the Scriabinesque tendencies of his pupil’s 1909 examination pieces: this was instruction accompanied by aesthetic friction, not agreement about what new music should sound like.

rimsky-korsakov--prokofiev-orchestration.title: Rimsky’s crowded orchestration classroom

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s St Petersburg Conservatory orchestration classes
works.to: Prokofiev’s student training

rimsky-korsakov--prokofiev-orchestration.claim: Prokofiev studied orchestration in Rimsky-Korsakov’s classes at the St Petersburg Conservatory. David Nice’s publisher biography also records his dissatisfaction with their crowded conditions, an important qualification to the easy picture of an intimate, contented master-and-disciple relationship.

debussy--bartok-kodaly-scores.title: Kodály brings Debussy’s scores to Bartók

works.from: Debussy’s scores, brought from Paris by Kodály
works.to: Bartók’s works from 1907

debussy--bartok-kodaly-scores.claim: Beginning in 1907 Bartók came under the influence of Debussy, whose compositions his friend Kodály had brought back from Paris. The discovery came as Bartók was already absorbed in collecting peasant music, so French harmony and Hungarian folk material reach his work together.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Béla Bartók

balakirev--ravel-scarbo-islamey.title: Scarbo aims beyond Islamey

works.from: Islamey
works.to: Gaspard de la nuit: Scarbo

balakirev--ravel-scarbo-islamey.claim: Ravel’s stated ambition for Scarbo was to go beyond the technical difficulty of Balakirev’s Islamey. The Russian work functions here as a challenge to surpass, not a theme to quote: repeated notes, leaps and rapid transformations become means of conjuring Bertrand’s elusive goblin.

Bethge’s German poems were paraphrases mediated by earlier European translations, including those of Judith Gautier and the Marquis d’Hervey-Saint-Denys, not direct translations made by Mahler from Chinese. works.to: Vaughan Williams’s Paris study, 1907–1908

Tom Service’s account of the surviving correspondence describes lessons directed at craft and clarity, including work with a Mozart minuet; the encounter did not require Vaughan Williams to abandon his own musical identity and become a French imitator.

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s teaching, St Petersburg

Soon afterwards Stravinsky met Sergei Diaghilev, who commissioned the ballets for the Ballets Russes that made his name.

works.from: Spanish songs sung by Ravel’s mother
works.to: Ravel’s Spanish musical world, including Rapsodie espagnole

The connection helps explain why Spanish subjects recur in his music, including Rapsodie espagnole; it does not identify every ostensibly Spanish melody as an actual childhood song quotation.

works.to: String Quartet No. 2, Op. 10, movements III–IV (1908)

stefan-george--schoenberg-quartet-2.claim: In the last two movements of his Second String Quartet, Schoenberg set poems by Stefan George for soprano, adding a voice to a genre that had never had one. The Rosé Quartet and the soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the first performance, and a critic of 1914 called the innovation Beethovenian, alluding to the choral finale of the Ninth Symphony.

wagner--debussy-golliwogg-tristan.title: Debussy mocks Tristan in a cakewalk

works.from: Tristan und Isolde, Prelude (1859)
works.to: Golliwogg’s Cakewalk, from Children’s Corner (1908)

wagner--debussy-golliwogg-tristan.claim: In Golliwogg’s Cakewalk, Debussy alludes satirically to Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde: the opening bars turn the Tristan chord into a jaunty, syncopated arpeggio, and the middle section is interrupted several times by a Tristan phrase marked avec une grande émotion. Debussy had heard the first act of Tristan at the Concerts Lamoureux in 1887 and judged it “decidedly the finest thing I know”, so the joke is aimed at a work he knew well.

The music’s recurring 5/8 motion accompanies an imagined crossing towards the island, but the illustration here is identified as a particular version, not asserted to be the exact reproduction he saw.

works.to: Suite aus den Orchesterwerken von J. S. Bach

works.from: Mahler’s conducting in New York

mahler--rachmaninoff-third-concerto-rehe.claim: Mahler conducted Rachmaninoff as soloist in the Third Piano Concerto in New York in January 1910, after its premiere under Walter Damrosch. Rachmaninoff later singled out Mahler’s painstaking rehearsal work: this connection between two favourites is documented collaboration over a new score, not a hypothetical stylistic resemblance.

works.to: Schoenberg’s contributions to the Blaue Reiter exhibition and almanac (1911–12)

kandinsky--schoenberg-blaue-reiter.claim: After hearing Schoenberg’s music at a Munich concert on 2 January 1911, Kandinsky wrote to him on 18 January: “In your works, you have realized what I, albeit in uncertain form, have so greatly longed for in music.” Schoenberg visited Kandinsky, Gabriele Münter and Franz Marc in Murnau, and the painters planned an exhibition and an almanac that drew in artists of every medium. The two corresponded until the First World War broke contact in 1914.

works.from: Gustav Mahler, who died in May 1911
works.to: Harmonielehre (1911)

mahler--schoenberg-harmonielehre.claim: Schoenberg wrote his Harmonielehre in the summer of 1910 and published it in 1911 with the dedication “Dem Andenken Gustav Mahlers ist dieses Buch geweiht” (“This book is dedicated to the memory of Gustav Mahler”). Mahler died on 18 May 1911, and the dedication makes the book Schoenberg’s memorial to him.

works.from: Concert of Schoenberg’s music, Munich (2 January 1911)
works.to: Impression III (Concert) (1911)

schoenberg--kandinsky-impression-iii.claim: Kandinsky’s painting Impression III (Concert) was inspired by a concert of Schoenberg’s works in Munich on 2 January 1911, which Kandinsky attended. He was so enthralled by the music that he wrote to Schoenberg within days, beginning an exchange of letters that lasted until 1914.

works.to: Valses nobles et sentimentales

schubert--ravel-valses-title.claim: Ravel explicitly linked the title Valses nobles et sentimentales with Schubert’s two named waltz collections. works.to: Three Japanese Lyrics (1912–13)

schoenberg--stravinsky-pierrot-lunaire.claim: In the winter of 1912 Stravinsky was in Berlin for performances of his ballets by the Ballets Russes, and attended a performance of Schoenberg’s Pierrot lunaire, conducted by the composer, less than two months after its premiere. works.to: The Rite of Spring, opening bassoon solo (1913)

Later scholars have identified several more melodies in Part I that came from the same Lithuanian collection, and Richard Taruskin’s study of the sketches traced further Russian folk sources.

works.to: The Bells, Op. 35

poe--rachmaninoff-bells-balmont.claim: Rachmaninoff’s choral symphony The Bells sets Konstantin Balmont’s free Russian adaptation of Poe, not Poe’s English poem directly. Its four movements pass through sleigh bells, wedding bells, alarm bells and funeral bells; Balmont’s changes, including an earlier presence of death, are part of the text Rachmaninoff actually composed.

basque-dance--ravel-piano-trio.title: The Trio sways in three-two-three

works.from: Basque dance rhythm
works.to: Piano Trio in A minor, movement I

basque-dance--ravel-piano-trio.claim: The first movement of Ravel’s Piano Trio groups its eight eighth notes as 3 + 2 + 3, a rhythm the Library of Congress programme note connects with Basque dance. Listen for unequal lengths rather than a conventional four-square pulse: the regional connection is rhythmic and need not imply a verbatim folk-tune quotation.

works.from: Woyzeck (play, 1837)
works.to: Wozzeck (opera, completed 1922)

buchner--berg-wozzeck.claim: In May 1914 Berg attended a performance in Vienna of Büchner’s play, left unfinished at the author’s death in 1837, and was moved to set it. The opera that followed, Wozzeck, kept the play’s fragmentary scenes in order and was completed after the First World War.

works.from: Poems by Francis Jammes
works.to: Clairières dans le ciel (1914)

jammes--lili-boulanger-clairieres.claim: Boulanger’s song cycle Clairières dans le ciel is set to poems by Francis Jammes. It stands with her three psalms for chorus and orchestra, the diptych D’un soir triste and D’un matin de printemps, and her Prix de Rome cantata Faust et Hélène among the works that made her reputation.

works.from: Symphony No. 5, opening motif (1808)
works.to: Piano Sonata No. 2, “Concord, Mass., 1840–60” (completed by 1915)

beethoven--ives-concord-sonata.claim: The opening bars of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony are quoted in each movement of Ives’s Concord Sonata, whose four movements portray Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau. Ives drew on material dating back to 1904, began substantial work around 1909 and largely completed the sonata by 1915; it was first published in 1920.

works.from: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes commissions
works.to: Ala et Lolly; Chout; Scythian Suite

diaghilev--prokofiev-rejected-ballet.claim: Diaghilev commissioned Ala et Lolly after meeting Prokofiev in 1914, then rejected the result and commissioned the Russian folk-tale ballet Chout instead. Prokofiev salvaged music from the rejected project as the Scythian Suite, so the impresario’s refusal helped redirect rather than simply terminate the material’s life.
