David Bray’s account identifies Znamenny chant in movements including No. 8, where altos and basses carry it in octaves, and No. 12; the surrounding choral texture gives a monodic tradition a many-voiced setting.

works.to: String Quartet No. 1, “Kreutzer Sonata” (1923)

tolstoy--janacek-kreutzer-quartet.claim: Janáček wrote his First String Quartet between 13 and 28 October 1923, inspired by Tolstoy’s novella The Kreutzer Sonata, which had itself been inspired by Beethoven’s violin sonata of that name. works.to: Turandot (1920–24, unfinished)

chinese-folk-melody--puccini-turandot.claim: Baron Edoardo Fassini-Camossi, a former Italian diplomat in China, gave Puccini a music box that played four Chinese melodies. Puccini worked three of them into Turandot, the most memorable being the folk melody “Mòlìhuā” (“Jasmine Flower”), which serves as a leitmotif for the princess’s splendour. In all, eight of the opera’s themes appear to be based on traditional Chinese music.

Webern keeps Bach’s notes and divides the lines among the instruments, so that melodies pass between colours: the principle he called Klangfarbenmelodie.

tolstoy--prokofiev-war-peace.claim: Prokofiev turned to Tolstoy’s War and Peace as an operatic project after the German invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941. His work with Mira Mendelson selected scenes from the novel rather than attempting to reproduce the entire book, and repeated revisions made the opera a continuing project rather than a score fixed once in 1941.

works.from: Symphony No. 3, “Eroica”, Marcia funebre (1804)
works.to: Metamorphosen (1945)

beethoven--richard-strauss-metamorphosen.claim: At the end of Metamorphosen, Strauss quotes the first four bars of the Marcia funebre from Beethoven’s Eroica Symphony and writes beneath them “IN MEMORIAM!”. A direct quotation from bar 3 of the march also appears earlier in the score as one of the work’s themes, so the funeral march is present throughout the piece before it is named at the close.

works.from: Messiaen’s private seminars and Conservatoire class

messiaen--boulez-harmony-class.claim: In June 1944 Boulez approached Messiaen and asked to study harmony with him. Messiaen invited him to attend the private seminars he gave to selected students, and in January 1945 Boulez joined his advanced harmony class at the Conservatoire de Paris. He also studied counterpoint privately with Andrée Vaurabourg and, with René Leibowitz, twelve-note technique.

works.from: Abdelazer, Rondeau (1695)
works.to: The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34 (1945)

purcell--britten-young-persons-guide.claim: Britten’s Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, subtitled Variations and Fugue on a Theme of Purcell, is based on the second movement, a rondeau, of Purcell’s Abdelazer suite. It was commissioned for the British educational documentary film Instruments of the Orchestra, released on 29 November 1946.

works.from: Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano (1946–48)

cage--boulez-sonatas-interludes.claim: Boulez’s friendship with John Cage began in 1949, when Cage was visiting Paris. Cage introduced him to two publishers, Heugel and Amphion, who agreed to take his recent pieces, and Boulez helped arrange a private performance of Cage’s Sonatas and Interludes for prepared piano.

works.from: The Well-Tempered Clavier (1722, 1742)
works.to: 24 Preludes and Fugues, Op. 87 (1950–51)

bach--shostakovich-leipzig-preludes-fugu.claim: In 1950 Shostakovich sat on the jury of the first International Johann Sebastian Bach Competition at Leipzig, held for the bicentenary of Bach’s death. The young Tatiana Nikolayeva from Moscow, who had come prepared to play any of the 48 preludes and fugues on request, won the gold medal. Inspired by the competition and her playing, he returned to Moscow and began his own cycle of 24 preludes and fugues, which Nikolayeva premiered in Leningrad on 23 December 1952.

works.to: Feldman’s graph pieces and Projections

cage--feldman-webern-lobby.claim: In January 1950 Feldman met John Cage walking out of Carnegie Hall, where both had gone to hear the New York Philharmonic under Dimitri Mitropoulos play Webern’s Symphony, Op. 21. Feldman soon moved into Cage’s apartment building on Grand Street, and through Cage met Jackson Pollock, Philip Guston and Frank O’Hara.

works.from: Birdsong, notated in the field
works.to: Le merle noir (1952); Réveil des oiseaux (1953)

birdsong--messiaen-oiseaux.claim: Messiaen was fascinated by birdsong and notated it around the world. Birds had appeared in several earlier works, but the flute piece Le merle noir was based entirely on the song of the blackbird; the orchestral Réveil des oiseaux (1953) took the idea further, its material consisting almost entirely of the birdsong one might hear between midnight and noon in the Jura. From then on he incorporated birdsong transcriptions into his compositions.

schoenberg--boulez-schoenberg-is-dead.title: Boulez declares “Schoenberg is Dead”

works.from: Schoenberg’s twelve-note music
works.to: “Schoenberg is Dead”, The Score (1952)

schoenberg--boulez-schoenberg-is-dead.claim: A 1952 article in the British journal The Score, published shortly after Schoenberg’s death, first brought Boulez international attention as a writer. In it he attacked Schoenberg for conservatism, contrasting him with the radicalism of Webern. The article caused widespread controversy, although Boulez had learned twelve-note technique privately with René Leibowitz, a champion of Schoenberg.

shostakovich--gubaidulina-mistaken-path.title: Shostakovich tells Gubaidulina to continue her “mistaken” way

works.from: Shostakovich’s verdict on a Conservatoire examination
works.to: Gubaidulina’s early music at the Moscow Conservatory

shostakovich--gubaidulina-mistaken-path.claim: Gubaidulina’s music was judged “irresponsible” during her studies at the Moscow Conservatory because it explored alternative tunings. When Shostakovich evaluated one of her examinations he encouraged her to continue on her path, although others, among them Tikhon Khrennikov, called it “mistaken”. She went on to the breakthrough of her violin concerto Offertorium in 1980.

mallarme--boulez-pli-selon-pli.title: Boulez folds Mallarmé’s sonnets into Pli selon pli

works.from: Sonnets by Stéphane Mallarmé
works.to: Pli selon pli, “Portrait de Mallarmé” (first performed 1960)

mallarme--boulez-pli-selon-pli.claim: Boulez’s Pli selon pli (“Fold by fold”), subtitled Portrait de Mallarmé, is a work in five movements for solo soprano and orchestra whose text is drawn from sonnets by Mallarmé. It was first performed in 1960 at Baden-Baden, sixty-six years after Debussy answered another Mallarmé poem with the Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune.

works.from: Silence: Lectures and Writings (1961)

cage--adams-silence.claim: Adams’s early work was aligned with modernist music, but he began to disagree with its tenets on reading John Cage’s Silence: Lectures and Writings. Teaching at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, he went on to develop a style of his own.

works.from: Ewe drumming taught by Gideon Alorwoyie, Legon (June 1970)

kafka--kurtag-kafka-fragments.claim: Kurtág’s Kafka-Fragmente, Op. 24 (1985–87), for soprano and violin, takes extracts from Kafka’s journals and letters and is broken into forty brief settings organised in four sections. Kurtág was fascinated by the bareness of Kafka’s language, by its sadness and despair, its humour and its depth. The soprano Adrienne Csengery and the violinist András Keller gave the first performance at the Witten Festival of Contemporary Chamber Music in 1987.

jaufre-rudel--saariaho-amour-de-loin.claim: Saariaho became familiar in 1993 with the twelfth-century troubadour Jaufré Rudel, the poet of far-off love (amor de lonh). She did not think herself capable of writing an opera until she saw Peter Sellars’s staging of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise at the 1992 Salzburg Festival. With a libretto by Amin Maalouf, L’Amour de loin (“Love from Afar”) was first performed at the Salzburg Festival on 15 August 2000.
